prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought the measurement of frequency to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part B009 configuration with exactly Katori and Ye, and the round-1 exchange has made my confidence in it firmer, not merely more comfortable. As chair I will say that unanimity after movement is not evidence, so I tested it against the chair's questions. On substance: the magic-wavelength lattice is a separable invention, because it removes the light shift that would otherwise forbid interrogating many trapped atoms at once, and that is the physical reason the statistical power exists for 10^-18 uncertainty. Ye's group then carried it to the systematic frontier and into many-body clock operation. Independent Sr and Yb realisations in several national laboratories, with intercontinental comparisons, mean the result does not depend on one group's claims. On delivered physics as distinct from prospective use, the clearest items are the resolution of the gravitational redshift across sub-millimetre height differences within one lattice-clock sample, and clock-ratio comparisons that now bound drifts of fundamental constants and ultralight dark-matter couplings. I treat the redshift result as demonstrated and the dark-matter reach as a limit-setting capability, and I say that plainly in the citation by crediting the invention and the accuracy level and nothing about future discoveries. On attribution, the split between the idea and the realisation is the cleanest on the shortlist, and the two-name configuration fits inside the limit of three people without tailoring anyone to fit.
statement.case_against: The category question is real and I do not dismiss it. The 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems cover the neighbouring lineage, and a sceptic can call a lattice clock a third helping of precision atomic physics. My answer is that the comb is the clockwork and ion control is a different route to accuracy, while the invention here is confinement of a neutral-atom ensemble without perturbing the transition, which neither earlier prize covers. That answer is a judgement, not a proof. The credit also necessarily leaves out the Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat, PTB and NIST contributions and the Yb and Hg communities, and the redefinition of the second has not been decided. If the committee decides it wants a prize that changes what physicists can think about rather than what they can measure, B009 loses ground to B018 or B052, and I would then want to discuss those on their merits and not pretend the clock is a discovery in the same sense. The remaining weakness I accept is that Danielsson's warning stands: breadth of ranking is not depth of scientific weight.

responses.point: Danielsson now prefers B009 but warns that eight rankings and six top-three placements make it the safe consensus pick, that the clocks have not yet produced a fundamental-physics result of their own, and that he wants more discussion of IceCube credit before placing it above the clock.
responses.response: I take his warning about safe consensus as the right test, and I tried to apply it to myself, since I opened with IceCube first. On his claim that no fundamental-physics result has come from the clocks, I would partly disagree: the redshift resolved across a millimetre-scale sample and the constraints from clock-ratio comparisons are results about nature and not about instrument performance, although I agree they are limits and tests and not discoveries of new physics. On B052, we now agree on the diagnosis. The diffuse flux is established, but a prize needs one credit allocation we can defend, and I do not think a Halzen, Karle, Spiering trio or my own Halzen and Karle pair is yet defensible against AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND. I have not changed my view of the science, only of how ready the committee is to write a citation.

responses.point: Olsson now prefers B009 with a citation that names magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms but not the 10^-18 level, and presses that if the committee took my view of IceCube it would have to justify excluding Spiering, which is not resolved.
responses.response: She is right that excluding Spiering is not resolved, and this is the main reason I have moved IceCube from my proposal to an alternative: I cannot defend a two-name or three-name split to the Academy on the record we have. I also agree with her wording instinct that the citation should anchor on trapping of neutral atoms, and I have moved my own citation toward it, but I would keep the 10^-18 level in the text because it states what the invention achieved and not what it promises. On B017 I remain where I was in round 1. Her disclosure about microscopy and her willingness to accept recusal are noted, and since B017 is not in my configuration I do not see it as a live issue for this round.

responses.point: Kroll argues that comb and ion-clock lineage belongs in the citation wording and not in a wider prize, that Katori's idea is separable from both, and discloses a doctoral-period link to John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, where Jun Ye also trained.
responses.response: I agree with his handling of the lineage and have written the citation so that it names the neutral-atom magic-wavelength mechanism and the accuracy level, which cannot be read as a claim about combs or ion clocks. On his disclosure, I think it should be recorded in the minutes and does not require recusal, because he describes a professional connection and no stake, and the committee has seven other members who reached the same ranking independently of him. If any member thought it material, abstention from the final ballot on B009 would be the proportionate step, not exclusion from the discussion. I also take his remark that B052 may deserve a prize soon, which I share.

responses.point: Lindroth could support a two-name Halzen and Karle version of IceCube if the committee went that way, but says B009 gives a cleaner, better-confirmed object today and would keep B052 for a later year.
responses.response: I appreciate the offer, and it is a fair statement of where the argument stands. The problem with a Halzen and Karle prize is the one Mehlig names: it departs from the three names supplied, and from my own side I do not want to appear to tailor the configuration to my first-ranked opening candidate. I also accept her point that the atomic-structure physics behind blackbody and polarisability corrections is part of why the performance claims are trustworthy, which answers the worry that the clock is only engineering. I agree with her that B009 is the better-confirmed object this year.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B010 second, holds that the clock support rests on merit and not convenience, and declines to tailor a trio to fit B052 if the committee settled on Halzen and Karle only.
responses.response: I share his reluctance to tailor a set of names and it is why I have not pressed my own two-name IceCube variant in this round. I still hold that B010 is a harder single part than B009, because Zoller's proposal, Greiner and Bloch's realisation and Esslinger's fermion experiments are separable and one must be omitted from a three-name limit, and Zoller's credit also overlaps B014. His point that the statistical-metrology argument is the physical reason the lattice works is one I accept and have used in my own case.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a discovery-class invention or as precision instrumentation after the 2005 and 2012 prizes; my answer rests on the neutral-atom confinement mechanism being a different step, which is a judgement.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second; I think the invention does not depend on that decision, but I cannot rule out that an adverse or delayed outcome would change how the prize reads.
Whether a citation can credit the idea and the accuracy frontier while stating that it does not credit other Sr, Yb and Hg groups, ion clocks or the comb.

For IceCube, whether the diffuse-flux discovery alone, without firm source identification, is sufficient, and how credit would be divided among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors.
I rely on my background knowledge of the history and results and cannot independently verify priority or internal credit within collaborations.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict for B009: my documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, KTH astroparticle physics) include no tie to Katori, Ye or atomic clocks. For B052 I repeat the field-proximity disclosure as an astroparticle experimentalist at KTH, with no recorded IceCube membership or tie to the credited names, and since B052 is now only an alternative I recommend no recusal. I have noted the disclosures by Kroll (Hall laboratory), Johansson (B008 field), Olsson (B017 field and IFSM role), Lindroth (atomic-physics bias) and Eriksson (electronic-structure proximity to B041 and B018); of these, I think Kroll's is the only one touching my preferred configuration and I would record it and not require recusal.
